name: Kaqchikel, Northern
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.

audit.action: check whether this is the same language as another entry
audit.recode_to: Merge into kaqc1270 (Kaqchikel) as duplicate entry, exactly as the sibling retired-code dialects kaqc1272/kaqc1276/kaqc1279 already were; same applies to kaqc1274 'Kaqchikel, Southern', which rests on the identical Berinstein quote. If a single Kaqchikel entry survives, its kind should be fixed-dominant (final) not fixed-strict: Bennett 2016:495 and ALMG 2004 document native non-final exceptions (janila, nana, tata, wakix, tukur) and penult-stressed Spanish loans; cite Rukemik 1997 Acento section / Bennett 2016 sec. 6.1 as deciding sources rather than Berinstein's background clause.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the three Berinstein 1979 passages exist verbatim at printed pp.47, vi, 52 (scanned of the open eScholarship scan downloaded now; no copy was held before). (2) The deciding source is a 1979 MA-thesis perception experiment whose stress claim is a background premise about 'Cakchiquel' generically; its 46 subjects came from Patzicia, Chimaltenango (p.47), which Ethnologue 15 places in the Central [cak] area, not the Northern [ckc] San Martin Jilotepeque area. So the record attributes to Northern Kaqchikel a statement that is neither dialect-specific nor drawn from Northern speakers. (3) kaqc1275 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping languoid for retired ISO ckc, merged into cak in 2009 (CR 2008-053 downloaded: 'dialects or dialect groups within a single language'); Glottolog lists zero descriptive references for it; by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) a retired code does not make a separate language, and three sibling

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (downloaded) (also digitized at HathiTrust, search-only (in copyright))
sources.quote: p. 47: "To distinguish these hypotheses the perception experiment was repeated with speakers of Cakchiquel, a related Mayan language, which has fixed final stress and no phonemic length." Also abstract p. vi: "Both K'ekchi and Cakchiquel have fixed final stress but they differ in that while K'ekchi has phonemic vowel length, Cakchiquel does not." And p. 52: "the final syllable (the normal location of stress) will be longer than any other syllable in the word."
